ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: In the rhombus $ABCD$ as shown in the figure, $AB=2$ and $\angle BAD=60^\circ$. The rhombus $ABCD$ is rotated counterclockwise around point $A$ to get the rhombus $AEFG$, where point $E$ is on $AC$, and $EF$ intersects $CD$ at point $P$. What is the length of $DP$?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:} As shown in the figure, connect BD intersecting AC at point O, \\
$\because$ Quadrilateral ABCD is a rhombus, \\
$\therefore$ CD=AB=2, $\angle$BCD=$\angle$BAD=$60^\circ$, $\angle$ACD=$\angle$BAC=$\frac{1}{2}\angle$BAD=$30^\circ$, OA=OC, AC$\perp$BD, \\
$\therefore$ OB=$\frac{1}{2}$AB=1, \\
$\therefore$ OA=$\sqrt{3}$OB=$\sqrt{3}$, \\
$\therefore$ AC=2OA=2$\sqrt{3}$, \\
By the property of rotation: AE=AB=2, $\angle$EAG=$\angle$BAD=$60^\circ$, \\
$\therefore$ CE=AC−AE=2$\sqrt{3}$−2, \\
$\because$ Quadrilateral AEFG is a rhombus, \\
$\therefore$ EF$\parallel$AG, \\
$\therefore$ $\angle$CEP=$\angle$EAG=$60^\circ$, \\
$\therefore$ $\angle$CEP+$\angle$ACD=$90^\circ$, \\
$\therefore$ $\angle$CPE=$90^\circ$, \\
$\therefore$ PE=$\frac{1}{2}$CE=$\sqrt{3}$−1, \\
$\therefore$ PC=$\sqrt{3}$PE=3−$\sqrt{3}$, \\
$\therefore$ DP=CD−PC=2−(3−$\sqrt{3}$)=$\boxed{\sqrt{3}-1}$.

raw_record.original_question: In the rhombus $ABCD$ as shown in the figure, $AB=2$ and $\angle BAD=60^\circ$. The rhombus $ABCD$ is rotated counterclockwise around point $A$ to get the rhombus $AEFG$, where point $E$ is on $AC$, and $EF$ intersects $CD$ at point $P$. What is the length of $DP$?
raw_record.answer:
Solution: As shown in the figure, connect $BD$ intersecting $AC$ at point $O$.
Because quadrilateral $ABCD$ is a rhombus,
therefore $CD=AB=2$, $\angle BCD=\angle BAD=60^\circ$, $\angle ACD=\angle BAC=\frac{1}{2}\angle BAD=30^\circ$, $OA=OC$, and $AC\perp BD$.
Therefore $OB=\frac{1}{2}AB=1$,
therefore $OA=\sqrt{3}OB=\sqrt{3}$,
therefore $AC=2OA=2\sqrt{3}$.
By the property of rotation: $AE=AB=2$, $\angle EAG=\angle BAD=60^\circ$,
therefore $CE=AC-AE=2\sqrt{3}-2$.
Because quadrilateral $AEFG$ is a rhombus,
therefore $EF\parallel AG$,
therefore $\angle CEP=\angle EAG=60^\circ$,
therefore $\angle CEP+\angle ACD=90^\circ$,
therefore $\angle CPE=90^\circ$,
therefore $PE=\frac{1}{2}CE=\sqrt{3}-1$,
therefore $PC=\sqrt{3}PE=3-\sqrt{3}$,
therefore $DP=CD-PC=2-(3-\sqrt{3})=\boxed{\sqrt{3}-1}$.
raw_record.final_cot: Image description: The attached diagram shows rhombus ABCD with A at the lower left, B at the lower right, C on the right, and D above-left of C. Diagonal AC is drawn. A second rhombus AEFG shares point A; E lies on segment AC, and side EF crosses side CD at point P. In the picture, P lies between D and C, so DP = CD - PC. Reasoning: In rhombus ABCD, AB = CD = 2 and ∠BAD = 60°. Since the sides adjacent to A are both 2 with included angle 60°, the diagonal AC has length AC = sqrt(2^2 + 2^2 + 2·2·2·cos60°) = sqrt(12) = 2√3. The rotation about A sends AB to AE, so AE = AB = 2. Since E lies on AC, CE = AC - AE = 2√3 - 2. In a rhombus, diagonal AC bisects the angle at C; because ∠BCD = ∠BAD = 60°, we get ∠ACD = 30°. In the rotated rhombus AEFG, EF ∥ AG, and ∠EAG = 60°. Since E is on AC, ∠CEP = 60°. Thus triangle CEP has angles 30°, 60°, and 90°, with CE as the hypotenuse. Therefore PC = (√3/2)CE = (√3/2)(2√3 - 2) = 3 - √3. Finally, CD = 2, so DP = CD - PC = 2 - (3 - √3) = √3 - 1.
